children: US crypto regulation has changed dramatically in 2025, as the Trump administration adopted a more pro-innovation and crypto-friendly approach. Since the start of 2026, the focus has shifted from major congressional reforms to new rules introduced by federal agencies.

This shift followed the CLARITY Act’s failure to pass the Senate. The bill aimed to create a clear regulatory framework for the crypto market, but its failure left regulators to move ahead using their existing powers.
As a result, the SEC and CFTC began introducing new rules, while banking regulators worked on implementing the GENIUS Act ahead of its January 18, 2027, effective date.
2026 Crypto Regulation Timeline: Key Federal and State Actions
January 29, 2026 —

CFTC Chairman Michael Selig declared an end to “regulation by enforcement” and joined SEC Chairman Paul Atkins to launch Project Crypto, a joint initiative aimed at harmonizing federal crypto oversight.
February 25, 2026 —
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
issued its initial proposed rule to implement the GENIUS Act for payment stablecoin issuers under its jurisdiction.
The SEC and CFTC signed a formal agreement establishing a framework for coordinating policies and sharing oversight responsibilities.
The SEC and CFTC issued a landmark joint interpretation classifying digital assets into five categories and defining when a crypto asset can separate from an investment contract.

The Virtual Currency Tax Fairness Act proposed a $300 tax-free limit on crypto purchases, while the Digital Asset PARITY Act sought to apply stock-style wash-sale rules. Neither passed, so crypto tax-loss harvesting remains allowed through 2026.
April 7, 2026 —
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) published proposed requirements for FDIC-supervised payment stablecoin issuers and insured depository institutions.
The National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) released a parallel proposed framework for credit unions seeking to issue payment stablecoins.

President Trump signed Executive Order 14405, titled Integrating Financial Technology Innovation into Regulatory Frameworks. He signed an order directing federal agencies to ease strict banking rules and support the use of digital assets in banking and payment systems.
The OCC, alongside the Treasury’s FinCEN and OFAC, published proposed rules applying Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering standards to stablecoin issuers.
August 18, 2026 —

The SEC proposed a 400-page standalone securities framework featuring two capital-raising exemptions and a conditional safe harbor that would allow certain non-security tokens to trade freely on secondary markets.
September 15, 2026 —

The Senate voted 49–50 against advancing the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, falling short of the 60 votes required to proceed. The bill stalled amid disputes over ethics provisions for federal officials and stablecoin yield rules.
September 29, 2026 —
The Federal Reserve Board published proposed rules outlining its supervisory responsibilities under the GENIUS Act.
October 13, 2026 —
CFTC published an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) proposing “Regulation CTX” and “Regulation CAM” to govern leveraged and margined retail crypto trading.
October 21, 2026 —
The OCC issued its final rule implementing the GENIUS Act, with the rule set to take effect on January 18, 2027.
November 3, 2026 —

Democrats won control of both the House and Senate for the new Congress beginning in January 2027. The result effectively put the CLARITY Act on hold for the remainder of the year and signaled greater congressional scrutiny of crypto regulators and bank charters.
November 6, 2026 —
FinCEN and the Federal Reserve withdrew a 2020 proposal to lower the cross-border Travel Rule and recordkeeping threshold for crypto transfers from $3,000 to $250.
What Do the U.S. Federal Agencies Think About Crypto in 2026?
In 2026, U.S. regulators have taken a more crypto-friendly approach, focusing on clearer rules and bringing digital assets into the traditional financial system.
SEC:

The SEC and CFTC clarified that most crypto assets are not securities on March 17, 2026. The SEC also proposed new rules to make it easier for crypto companies to raise funds and meet disclosure requirements.
CFTC:
The CFTC is working with the SEC to bring more crypto trading under U.S. oversight. It has also proposed new rules for digital commodity trading and derivatives.
FinCEN:
The Treasury and FinCEN dropped proposals that would have increased reporting requirements for crypto transfers involving private wallets and targeted crypto mixers.
FDIC, OCC, and Federal Reserve:

These banking regulators are working on rules to bring stablecoins into the traditional financial system under the GENIUS Act, which takes effect on January 18, 2027. They are also updating banking guidelines for institutions working with digital assets.
US Crypto Tax 202
Short-Term Crypto Tax Rates (Held ≤ 1 Year)

In the U.S., short-term capital gains on cryptocurrency held for one year or less (≤ 1 year) are taxed at your ordinary federal income tax rate, ranging from 10% to 37% for the 2026 tax year. Additional Crypto Tax Rules
Beyond capital gains, the IRS also taxes several crypto activities as ordinary income and requires detailed reporting and recordkeeping.
Ordinary Income
Staking and Mining:
Rewards are generally taxed as income when you receive them. Mining businesses may also face self-employment tax.
Airdrops and Hard Forks:
Tokens become taxable income once you have control over them.
Crypto Payments:
Crypto received as wages, freelance income, bonuses, or rewards is taxed as ordinary income.
DeFi Yield:
Interest and income earned through lending or liquidity pools are generally taxable when you receive them.
Who Uses the Most Crypto in the US?
According to a 2026 study by the Pew Research Center, 19% of all U.S. adults have ever invested in, traded, or used crypto, while 40% of men aged 30–49 and 38% of men aged 18–29 report using it.
Age & Generation:
Millennials (30–44) make up the largest share of crypto owners, while about two-thirds of U.S. holders are between 30 and 59.
Gender:
Men are more than twice as likely to use crypto as women (27% vs. 11%). However, women made up 42% of new crypto users in 2025–2026, narrowing the gap.
Income & Education:
Adoption is higher among upper-income adults (27%) than middle-income (20%) and lower-income groups (16%). About two-thirds of crypto investors have a bachelor’s degree or higher.
Race & Ethnicity:
Asian Americans have the highest adoption rate at 25%, followed by Black (20%), Hispanic (19%), and White (18%) adults.
Geography & Industry:
Adoption is strongest in major states such as California, Texas, Florida, and New York. Construction and manufacturing workers now match tech and finance workers, each accounting for 21% of holders.
Political Affiliation:
In 2026, Republicans reported higher crypto usage than Democrats, at 22% versus 17%.
Crypto Adoption Rate In America
Among U.S. crypto owners, Bitcoin remains the most popular asset at 74%, followed by Ethereum (53%), Dogecoin (25%), and Solana (20%).
Institutional & ETF Growth:
The U.S. remains the world’s largest crypto economy, with $2.78 trillion in transaction volume, driven by spot crypto ETFs, stablecoins, and tokenized assets.
Payments & Everyday Use:

About 39% of U.S. merchants accept crypto at checkout, rising to 50% among large businesses. Around 40% of crypto holders use digital assets for purchases, while 41% use them to send money to family and friends.
Barriers to Adoption:
For non-owners, volatility remains a major concern, with 37% citing price swings. Scams and fraud are an even bigger worry, reported by 72%.
Crypto Mining in the USA

As of November 2026, the U.S. remains the world’s largest Bitcoin mining hub, accounting for about 37.5% of global computing power, or roughly 360–400 EH/s. However, the industry is shifting as miners increasingly convert their power infrastructure into AI and high-performance computing (HPC) data centers.
Leading U.S. Miners in 2026
MARA Holdings:
The largest U.S. pure-play miner by active hashrate, with more than 70 EH/s. It mined 2,247 BTC in Q3 2026 and held 34,012 BTC.
Riot Platforms & CleanSpark:
Remain major U.S. mining operators, while also expanding into AI data centers and power infrastructure.
TeraWulf, Cipher Digital & Core Scientific:
Have gained market value through their AI and data-center strategies. Core Scientific has largely moved away from Bitcoin mining toward AI colocation.
IREN & Keel Infrastructure:

Are exiting Bitcoin mining to focus on AI infrastructure. IREN plans to significantly scale down mining by the end of 2026, while Keel has shut down its U.S. mining sites for AI data-center conversion.
DeFi in the US 2026

According to the October 2026 national study by the DeFi Education Fund and Ipsos, most Americans lack confidence in the traditional U.S. financial system and want greater personal control over their money and data.
• 40% of Americans say they are at least somewhat likely to try DeFi if clear access and frameworks are available (consistent with 42% in the prior wave).

• Among those likely to try DeFi, 85% said they would use it to “save money” (up from 77%), 82% said they would use it to “send money to friends or family” (up from 73%), and 82% said they would use it to “earn interest”.
• Nearly 7 in 10 Americans (69%) would use DeFi to receive a payment from work, retirement, or a government agency (up from 58%).
• Only 19% of Americans believe the existing U.S. financial system is secure, while 63% say it needs an upgrade and 74% say changes are needed to give people more control over their own assets
US Government’s Crypto Holdings
As of November 2026, the US government holds approximately 306,795 Bitcoins, valued at about $20.48 billion (part of a total crypto portfolio worth roughly $20.57 billion).
The US remains the world’s largest state holder of Bitcoin, with these assets coming from criminal and civil seizures, rather than open-market purchases.

Under President Trump’s March 2025 executive order, the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve now holds forfeited Bitcoin as a permanent national reserve, alongside about 17,432 ETH worth $33 million and $50+ million in other digital assets.
In late 2026, the government moved about $1.5 billion in holdings into institutional custody and secured court orders to seize more than $1.2 billion in stolen funds.
Conclusion

In 2026, U.S. crypto regulation moved toward greater institutional clarity, despite Congress failing to pass a comprehensive market-structure bill. The SEC and CFTC advanced new rules, while the GENIUS Act established a clearer framework for stablecoins.
New tax reporting requirements also strengthened compliance. However, major issues remain unresolved, including SEC-CFTC jurisdiction, DeFi regulation, and government Bitcoin purchases.

Overall, 2026 marked a shift from regulatory uncertainty toward broader institutional adoption, with the focus now moving to how crypto and traditional finance can operate within a clearer federal framework.
FAQs
Is crypto regulated by the SEC?

Yes, under current 2026 rules, the SEC oversees crypto assets that qualify as securities (or “investment contracts”), while decentralized commodities like Bitcoin fall primarily under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).
What are the IRS rules for crypto?
The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) classifies cryptocurrency and other digital assets as property, meaning every sale, swap, or spending event triggers a capital gain or loss.
What is the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve?
Established by Trump in March 2025, it’s a federal reserve for Bitcoin, initially capitalized by seized BTC, aiming to manage holdings strategically.
How has US crypto regulation changed in 2026?

In 2026, U.S. cryptocurrency regulation shifted from legislative promises to active agency rulemaking as the SEC and CFTC moved to write market rules after the Senate stalled broader crypto legislation.
How much tax on crypto USA?

In the US, short-term crypto gains (held ≤ 1 year) are taxed at ordinary income rates (10-37%), while long-term gains (> 1 year) are taxed at lower capital gains rates (0-20%), based on your income and filing status. Sources
